findings.impact: Withdrawal is the one lifecycle transition whose inherited T0 law adds a record obligation beyond the permission decision: it must append the reason and evidence to Registry authority, because withdrawal changes eligibility for all future execution selection while leaving immutable bytes and historical validity intact. The candidate carries the eligibility half of that law verbatim in section 7 and section 10 and drops the record half entirely. Its lifecycle fact now carries the resolved Product Authorization decision ref and, after the f30 closure, the predicate, profile, and clock-health evidence refs — all of which prove that the withdrawal was permitted and validly timed, none of which record why the release was withdrawn. The Product Authorization decision's own "stable reason code" per Product Authorization section 3 is the allow-or-deny reason, not the withdrawal reason, so it cannot substitute. A Registry satisfying all eighteen conformance items can therefore withdraw a release with no recorded reason, and Inspection, Contract Audit, and a later maintainer cannot distinguish a withdrawal for a discovered security defect from one for ordinary supersession — the exact judgment a withdrawal record exists to support. This omission is also invisible to the backstop revision 6 introduced: section 11's opening makes the ordering, atomicity, isolation, and evidence-recording rules of sections 7, 8, and 9 conformance obligations, which is why the unenumerated query and closure ports are still covered, but none of those three sections states the withdrawal record obligation, so nothing covers it. This is the same defect class as carried findings f21, f24, and f30 — a completion gate that passes while a declared owned result is absent — surviving on the one lifecycle axis those revisions did not examine.
